notes.front: What is the ArchiMate language and what is it for?
notes.back: An open, independent modeling language for Enterprise Architecture (EA), maintained by The Open Group. It provides uniform concepts and notation to describe, analyze, and visualize the architecture within and across business domains in an unambiguous way.
notes.extra: It supports EA development by enabling architects to model the construction and operation of business processes, organizational structures, information flows, IT systems, and technical/physical infrastructure — and the relationships and dependencies between them.

notes.front: Which layers of an Enterprise Architecture (EA) can be modeled with the ArchiMate language?
notes.back: The three core layers — Business, Application, and Technology — plus Strategy, Physical, and Implementation & Migration in the Full Framework, with the Motivation aspect crossing all layers.

A reference structure used to classify elements of the ArchiMate core language, consisting of three layers (Business, Application, Technology) and three aspects (Passive Structure, Behavior, Active Structure).
The central part of the ArchiMate language, defining the concepts to model Enterprise Architectures: the elements of the Business, Application, and Technology Layers and their relationships.
A representation of a system from the perspective of a related set of concerns.

A specification of the conventions for a particular kind of architecture view — the definition of what you should see and how (concepts, models, analysis techniques, visualizations) for a set of stakeholder concerns.
A classification of elements based on layer-independent characteristics related to the concerns of different stakeholders; the aspects are Passive Structure, Behavior, and Active Structure.
A property associated with an ArchiMate language element or relationship.
The generic term for either an element or a relationship in the ArchiMate language.
The fulfillment of specified requirements (of the ArchiMate specification).
An implementation that satisfies the conformance requirements defined by the conformance clause of the ArchiMate specification.
A structure or behavior element in one of the core layers (Business, Application, Technology) of the ArchiMate language.
An element consisting of other concepts, possibly from multiple aspects or layers of the language; Grouping and Product are examples.
A basic unit in the ArchiMate metamodel, used to define and describe the constituent parts of Enterprise Architectures and their unique set of characteristics.
An abstraction of the ArchiMate Framework at which an enterprise can be modeled.
A collection of concepts in the context of the ArchiMate language structure.
A connection between a source and target concept, classified as structural, dependency, dynamic, or other.

notes.front: Describe the top-level hierarchy of ArchiMate concepts
notes.back: Concept is the root; it specializes into Element, Relationship, and Relationship Connector. Element further specializes into Structure Element, Behavior Element, Motivation Element, and Composite Element.

notes.front: List the three layers of the ArchiMate core language
notes.back: Business Layer (business services realized by business processes performed by business actors), Application Layer (application services realized by software applications), and Technology Layer (technology services such as processing, storage, and communication, realized by computer/communication hardware and system software).
notes.extra: Layering follows a service orientation: each layer exposes services consumed by the layer above.

notes.front: What is the ArchiMate Core Framework?
notes.back: A 3×3 classification: three layers (Business, Application, Technology) × three aspects (Passive Structure, Behavior, Active Structure).

notes.front: What does the ArchiMate Full Framework add to the Core Framework?
notes.back: Three extra layers — Strategy, Physical, and Implementation & Migration — and the Motivation aspect, which crosses all layers.

notes.front: Explain the three aspects of the ArchiMate Core Framework
notes.back: Active Structure: elements that display actual behavior — the subjects of activity (who/what acts). Behavior: processes, functions, events, and services performed by actors (what happens). Passive Structure: objects on which behavior is performed — usually information or data objects, but also physical objects (what is acted upon).
notes.extra: Analogy with natural language: subject (active structure) — verb (behavior) — object (passive structure).

notes.front: Which forms of abstraction does the ArchiMate language distinguish?
notes.back: 1) External vs. internal view: services and interfaces (external) abstract from the internal elements that realize them. 2) Behavior vs. active structure: behavior can be modeled without knowing who performs it. 3) Conceptual–logical–physical: e.g., business object (conceptual) → data object (logical) → artifact (physical), linked by realization.

notes.front: Why does the ArchiMate specification separate concepts from notation?
notes.back: The semantics of concepts are defined independently of their graphical notation; the standard notation is one possible visualization. Tools may offer alternative notations for different stakeholders, as long as the meaning is preserved. A standard notation still matters for recognizability and unambiguous communication.

notes.front: What does nesting mean in an ArchiMate model?
notes.back: Placing one element graphically inside another as an alternative notation for a relationship between them — allowed for composition, aggregation, and assignment (and in views also for grouping). The relationship still exists in the model even when expressed by nesting.

notes.front: What are the ArchiMate color and notational-cue conventions?
notes.back: Colors are not formally part of the standard notation but are conventionally used to distinguish layers: yellow = Business, blue/cyan = Application, green = Technology (Physical shares green), tan/orange = Strategy, purple = Motivation, pink = Implementation & Migration. Shape cues ARE meaningful: square corners = structure elements, rounded corners = behavior elements, diagonal (cut) corners = motivation elements. A letter (M) marker can identify layers when color is absent.

notes.front: Sketch the generic metamodel: how do active structure, behavior, and passive structure relate?
notes.back: An internal active structure element is assigned to internal behavior; internal behavior realizes a service (external behavior); the active structure element composes an interface (external active structure) which is assigned to the service it exposes; behavior accesses passive structure elements; events trigger behavior.

notes.front: What is the difference between internal and external elements in the generic metamodel?
notes.back: External elements (services, interfaces) expose functionality to the environment and abstract from implementation; internal elements (processes, functions, components, actors) realize that functionality. A service is external behavior; an interface is external active structure — the access point where services are provided.

notes.front: What are the specializations of structure and behavior elements in the generic metamodel?
notes.back: Collaboration: an aggregate of two or more active structure elements working together (specialization of active structure). Interaction: a unit of collective behavior performed by a collaboration (specialization of behavior). These exist in the Business, Application, and Technology Layers.

notes.front: Which composite elements does the ArchiMate language define?
notes.back: Grouping — aggregates or composes concepts that belong together based on some common characteristic (drawn as a dashed rectangle with a tab); and Location — a place or position where structure elements can be located or behavior can be performed.

notes.front: List the four categories of ArchiMate relationships (and the connector)
notes.back: 1) Structural: composition, aggregation, assignment, realization — model the static construction or composition of concepts. 2) Dependency: serving, access, influence, association — model how elements support or are used by other elements. 3) Dynamic: triggering, flow — model temporal/causal dependencies and transfers between behavior. 4) Other: specialization. Plus the relationship connector: junction (and/or).
Represents that an element consists of one or more other concepts — a whole-part relationship where the part can belong to only one whole and cannot exist independently of it.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Filled diamond at the end of the WHOLE (composer). Nesting is an alternative notation.

notes.back: Represents that an element combines one or more other concepts — a whole-part relationship where the part may belong to multiple wholes and can exist independently.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Open (hollow) diamond at the end of the whole. Nesting is an alternative notation.

notes.back: Represents the allocation of responsibility, performance of behavior, storage, or execution — e.g., a business role assigned to a business process, an application component assigned to an application function, an artifact deployed on a node.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Filled ball at the source (active element), filled arrowhead at the target.

notes.back: Represents that an entity plays a critical role in the creation, achievement, sustenance, or operation of a more abstract entity — e.g., a business process realizes a business service; a data object realizes a business object.
notes.extra:
Line style: dotted line

Dotted line with hollow (open) triangle pointing at the more abstract (realized) element.

notes.back: Represents that an element provides its functionality to another element — e.g., an application service serves a business process; a business interface serves a business actor.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Solid line with open (line) arrowhead pointing at the element being served (the consumer). Called 'used by' in older ArchiMate versions.

notes.back: Represents the ability of behavior and active structure elements to observe or act upon passive structure elements — e.g., a business process accesses a business object.
notes.extra:
Line style: dotted line

Dotted line; arrowhead points at the passive element for write, at the accessor for read, both ends for read/write, no arrowhead for unspecified access.

notes.back: Represents that an element affects the implementation or achievement of some motivation element — e.g., a goal positively or negatively influences another goal. Strength can be annotated (e.g., +, ++, −, 0..10).
notes.extra:
Line style: dashed line

Dashed line with open arrowhead; the only relationship whose target must be a motivation element. Used mainly between motivation elements.

notes.back: Represents an unspecified relationship, or one that is not represented by another ArchiMate relationship.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Plain solid line; a directed association has a half arrowhead at the target (e.g., applied-to end of a contract, source of data in a flow specification).

notes.back: Represents a temporal or causal relationship between elements — e.g., one business process triggers the next, or a business event triggers a business process.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Solid line with filled arrowhead at the successor.

notes.back: Represents transfer from one element to another — of information, goods, money, or value — e.g., a flow of order data between two processes.
notes.extra:
Line style: dashed line

Dashed line with filled arrowhead; can be labeled with what is transferred.

notes.back: Represents that an element is a particular kind of another element of the same type — e.g., 'Take out travel insurance' specializes the process 'Take out insurance'.
notes.extra:
Line style: solid line

Solid line with hollow triangle pointing at the more GENERAL element. The only relationship allowed between two elements of the same type in all cases.

notes.front: What is a junction, and what is the difference between an and-junction and an or-junction?
notes.back: A relationship connector used to combine or split relationships of the same type (typically dynamic relationships such as triggering or flow, but also others except specialization). A filled circle is an and-junction (all paths); an open circle is an or-junction (a choice between paths).

notes.front: Recognize: open-circle connector splitting a triggering relationship
notes.back: An or-junction — models a choice: exactly one (or some) of the connected paths is taken.

notes.front: Rank the structural relationships from strongest to weakest (relevant for derivation)
notes.back: Composition (strongest) → Aggregation → Assignment → Realization. Among dependency relationships: Serving → Access → Influence → Association (weakest).
notes.extra: This ordering drives the derivation rule for valid relationships: a chain may be replaced by its weakest relationship.

notes.front: Which line styles do the ArchiMate relationships use? (dotted vs dashed vs solid)
notes.back: Solid: composition, aggregation, assignment, serving, association, triggering, specialization. Dotted: realization, access. Dashed: flow, influence.

notes.front: Sketch the structure of the motivation elements metamodel
notes.back: Stakeholders have drivers (associations); assessments analyze drivers; assessments and drivers influence goals; outcomes realize goals; principles, requirements, and constraints realize goals (requirements realize principles; constraint is a specialization of requirement). Meaning and value can be associated with any element.
The role of an individual, team, or organization (or classes thereof) that represents their interests in the effects of the architecture.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Examples: board, CEO (Chief Executive Officer), customer, regulator.

notes.back: An external or internal condition that motivates an organization to define its goals and implement the changes necessary to achieve them.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Examples: customer satisfaction, regulatory change, profitability.

notes.back: The result of an analysis of the state of affairs of the enterprise with respect to some driver.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Example: 'Customers complain about waiting times' — often a SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) outcome.

notes.back: A high-level statement of intent, direction, or desired end state for an organization and its stakeholders.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Example: 'Increase customer satisfaction by 10%'.

notes.back: An end result, effect, or consequence of a certain state of affairs.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Outcomes realize goals; results are tangible, possibly quantitative. Example: 'First-contact resolution rate raised to 90%'.

notes.back: A statement of intent defining a general property that applies to any system in a certain context in the architecture.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Broader than a requirement: normative for ALL systems in a context (e.g., 'Data is stored only in EU data centers'); realized by requirements.

notes.back: A statement of need defining a property that applies to a specific system as described by the architecture.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Realizes goals/principles for a SPECIFIC system.

notes.back: A limitation on aspects of the architecture, its implementation process, or its realization.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Specialization of requirement — restricts HOW, e.g., budget, deadline, or mandated technology.

notes.back: The knowledge or expertise present in, or the interpretation given to, a concept in a particular context.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Typically associated with a business object or representation.

notes.back: The relative worth, utility, or importance of a concept.
notes.extra:
Layer: Motivation

Aspect: Motivation

Often attached to services or products; can be associated with any element.

notes.front: How are motivation elements related to core elements?
notes.back: Core elements realize motivation elements: a requirement (or constraint) is realized by a core element such as a business process, application component, or service, and via the chain requirement → goal the whole architecture is traced back to intent. Influence and association also connect motivation and core elements (e.g., value associated with a service). The key exam relationship is REALIZATION from core elements to requirements.

notes.front: Sketch the structure of the strategy elements metamodel
notes.back: Resources are assigned to capabilities; capabilities (and resources) realize courses of action; capabilities serve value streams; strategy elements realize motivation elements (e.g., a course of action realizes goals) and are realized by core elements.
An asset owned or controlled by an individual or organization.
notes.extra:
Layer: Strategy

Aspect: Structure (passive/active)

Tangible (people, machines, money) or intangible (brand, data). Square corners: structure element.

notes.back: An ability that an active structure element, such as an organization, person, or system, possesses.
notes.extra:
Layer: Strategy

Aspect: Behavior

Rounded corners: behavior element. Typically realized by people, processes, and technology in combination.

notes.back: A sequence of activities that create an overall result for a customer, stakeholder, or end user.
notes.extra:
Layer: Strategy

Aspect: Behavior

Added in ArchiMate 3.1. Stages are modeled as value streams composed/aggregated of value streams, connected by flow; capabilities serve value stream stages.

notes.back: An approach or plan for configuring some capabilities and resources of the enterprise, undertaken to achieve a goal.
notes.extra:
Layer: Strategy

Aspect: Behavior

Strategy or tactic; realized by capabilities and resources, realizes goals/outcomes.

notes.back: A business actor is assigned to a business role; the role is assigned to business behavior (process/function/interaction); behavior realizes business services, which are exposed through business interfaces; behavior accesses business objects; business events trigger behavior; products aggregate services, objects, and a contract.
A business entity that is capable of performing behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Active Structure

A person, department, or organization — performs behavior via assigned roles.

notes.back: The responsibility for performing specific behavior, to which an actor can be assigned, or the part an actor plays in a particular action or event.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Active Structure

Decouples WHO (actor) from the responsibility (role); actor —assignment→ role —assignment→ process.

notes.back: An aggregate of two or more business internal active structure elements that work together to perform collective behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Active Structure

Performs business interactions; often temporary.

notes.back: A point of access where a business service is made available to the environment.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Active Structure (external)

A channel: phone desk, web chat, branch office. Same 'lollipop' icon as other interfaces.

notes.back: A sequence of business behaviors that achieves a specific result such as a defined set of products or business services.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior

Ordered ('how'); icon is an arrow. Compare business function (grouped by criteria).

notes.back: A collection of business behavior based on a chosen set of criteria (such as required business resources and/or competencies), closely aligned to an organization, but not necessarily explicitly governed by the organization.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior

Grouped by skills/resources ('what'), stable over time; processes typically use multiple functions.

notes.back: A unit of collective business behavior performed by (a collaboration of) two or more business roles.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior

Performed by a business collaboration.

notes.back: An organizational state change.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior

Something that happens (internally or externally) and may trigger or be triggered/thrown by behavior; instantaneous or with duration. Example: 'Claim received'.

notes.back: Explicitly defined behavior that a business role, business actor, or business collaboration exposes to its environment.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Behavior (external)

External view: hides internal processes; provides value to the consumer.

notes.back: A concept used within a particular business domain.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Passive Structure

Informational/conceptual, e.g., 'Invoice', 'Insurance Policy'; realized by data objects or representations.

notes.back: A formal or informal specification of an agreement between a provider and a consumer that specifies the rights and obligations associated with a product and establishes functional and non-functional parameters for interaction.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Passive Structure

Specialization of business object; part of a product.

notes.back: A perceptible form of the information carried by a business object.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Passive Structure

E.g., a printed bill or a PDF (Portable Document Format) form; realizes a business object.

notes.back: A coherent collection of services and/or passive structure elements, accompanied by a contract/set of agreements, which is offered as a whole to (internal or external) customers.
notes.extra:
Layer: Business

Aspect: Composite

Composite element: aggregates business/application/technology services, objects, and a contract. Example: 'Travel insurance' product.

notes.back: An application component is assigned to application behavior (function/process/interaction); behavior realizes application services exposed through application interfaces (composed by the component); behavior accesses data objects; application events trigger behavior; application collaborations perform application interactions.
An encapsulation of application functionality aligned to implementation structure, which is modular and replaceable.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Active Structure

A whole application or modular part of it; the UML (Unified Modeling Language) component icon with two tabs.

notes.back: An aggregate of two or more application internal active structure elements that work together to perform collective application behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Active Structure

E.g., front-end and back-end components jointly handling a transaction.

notes.back: A point of access where application services are made available to a user, another application component, or a node.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Active Structure (external)

E.g., an API (Application Programming Interface) or a GUI (Graphical User Interface).

notes.back: Automated behavior that can be performed by an application component.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior

Internal behavior grouped by functionality; realizes application services.

notes.back: A unit of collective application behavior performed by (a collaboration of) two or more application components.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior

notes.back: A sequence of application behaviors that achieves a specific result.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior

Ordered automated behavior, e.g., a straight-through claims-processing flow.

notes.back: An application state change.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior

E.g., 'message received'; may trigger application behavior.

notes.back: An explicitly defined exposed application behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Behavior (external)

Serves business processes/functions or other application components.

notes.back: Data structured for automated processing.
notes.extra:
Layer: Application

Aspect: Passive Structure

Logical data; realizes business objects, realized by artifacts.

notes.back: Nodes (devices, system software) are assigned to technology behavior (function/process/interaction); behavior realizes technology services exposed through technology interfaces; behavior accesses artifacts; artifacts are assigned to (deployed on) nodes; paths and communication networks connect nodes; technology events trigger behavior.
A computational or physical resource that hosts, manipulates, or interacts with other computational or physical resources.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Generic infrastructure resource; devices and system software are specializations.

notes.back: A physical IT (Information Technology) resource upon which system software and artifacts may be stored or deployed for execution.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Specialization of node: server, router, smartphone.

notes.back: Software that provides or contributes to an environment for storing, executing, and using software or data deployed within it.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Specialization of node: operating system, DBMS (Database Management System), application server, container runtime.

notes.back: An aggregate of two or more technology internal active structure elements that work together to perform collective technology behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

E.g., a cluster of nodes jointly providing failover.

notes.back: A point of access where technology services offered by a node can be accessed.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure (external)

E.g., a network port, a management API (Application Programming Interface).

notes.back: A link between two or more nodes, through which these nodes can exchange data, energy, or material.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Logical communication link; realized by one or more networks.

notes.back: A set of structures that connects nodes for transmission, routing, and reception of data.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Active Structure

Physical communication medium, e.g., a LAN (Local Area Network); realizes paths.

notes.back: A collection of technology behavior that can be performed by a node.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior

notes.back: A sequence of technology behaviors that achieves a specific result.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior

E.g., an automated backup or deployment procedure.

notes.back: A unit of collective technology behavior performed by (a collaboration of) two or more nodes.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior

notes.back: A technology state change.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior

E.g., 'disk full', 'message arrived'.

notes.back: An explicitly defined exposed technology behavior.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Behavior (external)

E.g., messaging, storage, or processing services serving application components.

notes.back: A piece of data that is used or produced in a software development process, or by deployment and operation of an IT (Information Technology) system.
notes.extra:
Layer: Technology

Aspect: Passive Structure

E.g., a container image, WAR (Web Application Archive) file, configuration file; realizes data objects and application components; assigned to (deployed on) nodes.

notes.back: One or more physical machines, tools, or instruments that can create, use, store, move, or transform materials.
notes.extra:
Layer: Physical

Aspect: Active Structure

Specialization of node; e.g., an assembly robot or a bottling machine.

notes.back: A physical structure or environment.
notes.extra:
Layer: Physical

Aspect: Active Structure

E.g., a factory, warehouse, or data center; often composes/aggregates equipment.

notes.back: A physical network used to transport materials or energy.
notes.extra:
Layer: Physical

Aspect: Active Structure

Physical counterpart of the communication network; e.g., rail network, power grid, pipeline.

notes.back: Tangible physical matter or physical elements.
notes.extra:
Layer: Physical

Aspect: Passive Structure

E.g., raw materials, fuel, paper; accessed by physical/technology behavior.

notes.front: How do the physical elements relate to the Technology Layer?
notes.back: Physical elements are an extension of the Technology Layer (same green color, no separate behavior elements): equipment is a specialization of node, so technology behavior elements (function, process, interaction, event, service) are used to model the behavior of physical elements; material is the physical passive structure element accessed by that behavior.
An element that aggregates or composes concepts that belong together based on some common characteristic.
notes.extra:
Layer: Composite (layer-independent)

Aspect: Composite

Dashed rectangle with a tab; can group any concepts, including relationships between groupings. Aggregation (default) or composition semantics.

notes.back: A place or position where structure elements can be located or behavior can be performed.
notes.extra:
Layer: Composite (layer-independent)

Aspect: Composite

Typically connected with an aggregation relationship (or assignment) to the located elements.

notes.front: Which two relationships primarily align the Business Layer with lower layers?
notes.back: Serving: an application service serves business processes, functions, interactions, or events (and application interfaces serve business roles). Realization: e.g., a data object realizes a business object; an application process/function may realize a business process/service (abstraction across layers).
notes.extra: Aggregation is also used across layers inside a product: a product may aggregate application and technology services and data objects.

notes.front: Which relationships align the Application and Technology Layers?
notes.back: Serving: technology services serve application components/functions. Realization: artifacts realize application components and data objects; technology processes/functions may realize application services. Assignment is used to deploy artifacts on nodes.

notes.front: How can the Business Layer be connected to the Technology Layer directly?
notes.back: Through derived relationships: e.g., if a node is assigned to an artifact that realizes an application component whose service serves a business process, a derived dependency (serving) from the technology element to the business element can be shown, following the derivation rules.

notes.front: Sketch the Implementation & Migration elements metamodel
notes.back: Implementation events trigger work packages; work packages realize deliverables; deliverables realize plateaus; a gap is associated with two plateaus (the difference between them). Standard relationships apply throughout.
A series of actions identified and designed to achieve specific results within specified time and resource constraints.
notes.extra:
Layer: Implementation & Migration

Aspect: Behavior

A project, program, or task; realizes deliverables.

notes.back: A precisely-defined result of a work package.
notes.extra:
Layer: Implementation & Migration

Aspect: Passive Structure

E.g., a report, a deployed system, a migrated database.

notes.back: A state change related to implementation or migration.
notes.extra:
Layer: Implementation & Migration

Aspect: Behavior

E.g., 'project kick-off', 'go-live'; triggers or is raised by work packages; may be associated with a plateau start/end.

notes.back: A relatively stable state of the architecture that exists during a limited period of time.
notes.extra:
Layer: Implementation & Migration

Aspect: Composite

Baseline, transition, and target architectures are modeled as plateaus.

notes.back: A statement of difference between two plateaus.
notes.extra:
Layer: Implementation & Migration

Aspect: Passive Structure

Associated with the two plateaus it separates; central to gap analysis in migration planning.

notes.front: How do Implementation & Migration elements relate to the core, composite, and motivation aspects?
notes.back: Deliverables realize core elements (the new/changed architecture content); plateaus aggregate core elements valid in that state; work packages can be assigned resources and realize requirements/goals; gaps are associated with the core elements that differ between plateaus; implementation events can trigger business events and vice versa.

notes.front: Stakeholder vs. concern — define both (views context)
notes.back: Stakeholder: individual, team, or organization (or classes thereof) with interests in, or concerns relative to, a system. Concern: an interest in a system relevant to one or more of its stakeholders — e.g., performance, cost, security, compliance.

notes.front: What is the difference between an architecture view and an architecture viewpoint?
notes.back: A VIEW is what you see: a representation of a system from the perspective of a related set of concerns — the content. A VIEWPOINT is where you look from: the specification of conventions (concepts, notation, analysis techniques) for constructing and using a view. A view is governed by a viewpoint; a view is an instance, the viewpoint its definition.

notes.front: Describe the conceptual model of an architecture description (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010)
notes.back: A system has stakeholders with concerns; an architecture description consists of views; each view is governed by exactly one viewpoint; a viewpoint frames one or more concerns; views are composed of models. The ArchiMate viewpoint mechanism implements this International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 42010 framework.

notes.front: Name the four categories of example viewpoints in the ArchiMate specification
notes.back: Basic viewpoints (e.g., Organization, Application Structure, Technology, Layered, Product, Service Realization); Motivation viewpoints (Stakeholder, Goal Realization, Requirements Realization, Motivation); Strategy viewpoints (Strategy, Capability Map, Value Stream, Outcome Realization, Resource Map); Implementation & Migration viewpoints (Project, Migration, Implementation and Migration).

notes.front: Describe the two levels of the ArchiMate 3 Certification for People program
notes.back: Level 1 — ArchiMate 3 Foundation: knowledge of the notation, terminology, structure, and basic concepts of the language; achieved by completing the Level 1 Learning Units and passing the Part 1 exam. Level 2 — ArchiMate 3 Practitioner: adds the ability to APPLY the language; requires Level 1 + Level 2 Learning Units and passing both Part 1 and Part 2 exams. Certification does not expire.

notes.front: ArchiMate 3 Part 1 exam: format, duration, pass mark, open book?
notes.back: 40 simple multiple-choice questions, 60 minutes, closed book, supervised. One point per correct answer; pass mark 60% (24 of 40). Aligned with the ArchiMate 3.2 Specification.

notes.front: ArchiMate 3 Part 2 exam: format, scoring, pass mark, open book?
notes.back: 8 complex scenario questions with gradient scoring: best answer 5 points, second-best 3, third 1, distracter 0 (max 40). 90 minutes, supervised, OPEN BOOK — an electronic copy of the ArchiMate specification is built into the exam. Pass mark 65% (26 of 40). Prerequisite: ArchiMate 3 Foundation, or passing Part 1 the same day at the same test center.
notes.extra: Failed an ArchiMate exam? One-month wait before any retake.

notes.front: State the derivation rule for valid relationships (structural/dependency chains)
notes.back: A chain of structural and/or dependency relationships in the same direction may be replaced by the WEAKEST relationship in the chain. Strength (strong→weak): composition, aggregation, assignment, realization, serving, access, influence, association.
notes.extra: Example: component —assignment→ function —realization→ service ⇒ derived component —realization→ service.

notes.front: Derivation: role R is assigned to process P; P realizes service S. What can be derived between R and S?
notes.back: Assignment and realization are both structural; the weaker of the two is realization — so a derived REALIZATION from role R to service S is valid.

notes.front: Derivation: application service A serves business process B; B is composed in process C... what about chains that include serving?
notes.back: Serving is weaker than all structural relationships, so a chain mixing structural relationships and serving derives to serving (or weaker). E.g., component —assignment→ function —serving→ process derives component —serving→ process.

notes.front: What is the difference between valid and potential derived relationships?
notes.back: Valid derivations ALWAYS hold — mechanically derived from chains of structural/dependency relationships using the weakest-link rule. Potential derivations MAY hold — they involve dynamic relationships (triggering, flow) or specific patterns (e.g., derived triggering across assigned behavior, flow between active elements assigned to behaviors that exchange flow), and require modeler judgment about whether they apply.

notes.front: Give an example of a potential derivation involving flow
notes.back: If role A is assigned to process P1, role B to process P2, and there is a flow from P1 to P2, then a POTENTIAL flow between A and B can be derived (the roles exchange something via their processes) — but it need not hold in every interpretation.

notes.front: Name a restriction on applying derivation rules
notes.back: Derivation must respect relationship direction; no valid derivation ends in a stronger relationship than any link in the chain; specialization requires source and target of the same element type; derived relationships must still be allowed by the relationship tables (Appendix B) between the source and target element types.

notes.front: Explain service orientation across the ArchiMate layers (Level 2 depth)
notes.back: Each layer exposes services to the layer(s) above: technology services serve application components; application services serve business behavior; business services serve the environment/customers. Layers are linked by serving (use of services) and realization (elements in a lower layer realize comparable, more abstract elements in a higher layer). This creates a layered view from customer-facing value down to infrastructure.

notes.front: Explain the conceptual–logical–physical abstraction chain with a concrete modeling example
notes.back: Conceptual: business object 'Customer file' (information as the business sees it). Logical: data object 'Customer record' realizes the business object (structured for processing). Physical: artifact 'customers.db' realizes the data object (concrete file deployed on a node). The same pattern applies to behavior: business process ← application process ← technology process via realization.

notes.front: Practical pattern: model 'regulator demands shorter response times, so we aim to cut handling time 30%, met by a new claims process'
notes.back: Stakeholder 'Regulator' — association — driver 'Regulatory compliance'; assessment 'Response times too long' — influence → goal 'Cut handling time 30%'; requirement 'Automate claim intake' realizes the goal; business process 'Handle claim (new)' realizes the requirement.

notes.front: Practical pattern: connect strategy to execution (capability-based planning)
notes.back: Course of action 'Digital-first distribution' realizes goal; capability 'Online sales' realizes the course of action; resource 'E-commerce platform team' is assigned to the capability; core elements (business processes, application services) realize the capability; capabilities serve value stream stages such as 'Acquire customer'.

notes.front: Resource vs. Capability vs. Course of Action vs. Value Stream — distinguish in one line each
notes.back: Resource: an asset you HAVE (owned/controlled). Capability: an ability you CAN exercise (what you can do, not how). Course of action: a plan you CHOOSE (how capabilities/resources will be configured to reach a goal). Value stream: value-creating activities you PERFORM end-to-end for a customer/stakeholder.

notes.front: Business process vs. business function — when do you model which?
notes.back: Process: ordered sequence of behavior producing a defined result, often crossing functions/departments ('Handle claim'). Function: behavior clustered by required skills, resources, or competences, stable over time ('Claims administration', 'Finance'). Typical pattern: processes USE (are served by) functions, or functions aggregate the behavior that processes orchestrate.

notes.front: Business actor vs. business role — exam-typical scenario reasoning
notes.back: Model the responsibility as a ROLE ('Claims assessor') and the concrete entity as an ACTOR ('Jane Doe', 'Claims department'), with actor —assignment→ role —assignment→ process. This lets the organization change who fulfills a responsibility without remodeling the behavior.

Application component composes its interfaces; component assigned to application function; function realizes application service; service serves business process; function accesses data objects; data object realizes business object.

notes.front: Typical deployment pattern in the Technology Layer
notes.back: Artifact 'app-v2.1.jar' realizes application component 'Policy admin'; artifact is assigned to (deployed on) node 'App server' (or system software 'Java Runtime Environment (JRE)' assigned to device); node composes technology interface; technology service 'Hosting' realized by node behavior serves the application component; nodes connected by paths realized by communication networks.

notes.front: How do you model a transition architecture roadmap in ArchiMate?
notes.back: Plateaus for baseline, transition(s), and target; gaps associated with each pair of consecutive plateaus; work packages (projects) realize deliverables; deliverables realize the plateaus (or the core elements aggregated by them); implementation events mark milestones; goals/requirements linked via realization show why each transition exists.

notes.front: How are viewpoints classified by PURPOSE in the ArchiMate specification?
notes.back: Designing: support architects/designers in design activities (typical: diagrams, detailed models). Deciding: support managers in decision-making (cross-reference tables, landscape maps, analyses). Informing: inform stakeholders to obtain understanding and commitment (illustrations, animations, simplified views).

notes.front: How are viewpoints classified by CONTENT (abstraction level)?
notes.back: Details: one layer and one aspect, for designers/engineers (e.g., a single process or application). Coherence: multiple layers OR multiple aspects, for operational managers (e.g., process-uses-system). Overview: multiple layers AND multiple aspects, for enterprise architects and general management.

notes.front: What are the steps to define and use an architecture viewpoint?
notes.back: 1) Identify stakeholders and their concerns; 2) scope the viewpoint: select the relevant layers, aspects, concepts, relationships, and depth (purpose + content classification); 3) define conventions/notation for the view; 4) create the view by selecting model elements (applying derivation rules where needed to hide intermediate elements); 5) validate with the stakeholders that their concerns are addressed.

notes.front: What are the two language customization mechanisms in the ArchiMate specification?
notes.back: 1) Adding attributes to elements and relationships via profiles — a profile is a coherent set of attributes (name + type) that can be attached to concepts; pre-defined or user-defined. 2) Specialization of elements and relationships — defining new concepts as particular kinds of existing ones.

notes.front: What is allowed when you specialize an ArchiMate element?
notes.back: The specialized element inherits the characteristics (allowed relationships) of its generalization; you may denote it with a stereotype-like label in guillemets («specialization»), and you may add or change its graphical notation (new icons, markers, colors) as long as it stays recognizable. Relationships can be specialized too (e.g., a «hosts» assignment).
notes.extra: Profiles + specialization together support domain-specific extensions and quantitative analysis (e.g., cost or performance attributes).

notes.back: Composition: exclusive whole-part — a part belongs to exactly one whole (filled diamond). Aggregation: shared whole-part — a part can belong to multiple wholes and exist independently (open diamond).

Serving: provides functionality TO another element (support during operation; solid line, open arrow to consumer). Realization: brings a more abstract element INTO EXISTENCE / makes it work (dotted line, hollow triangle to the abstract element). A process REALIZES a service; that service SERVES its consumers.

Triggering: temporal/causal order — A causes/precedes B (solid, filled arrow). Flow: transfer of information, goods, money, or value — something moves from A to B (dashed, filled arrow). Flow does not imply causation or order.

Access: only between behavior/active structure and PASSIVE structure elements; expresses read/write semantics (dotted). Association: any unspecified relationship between any concepts (solid, no or half arrowhead).

notes.front: Goal vs. Outcome vs. Requirement — distinguish
notes.back: Goal: desired direction/end state (intent). Outcome: achieved end result (fact, often measured) that realizes goals. Requirement: property a SPECIFIC system must have to realize goals/principles.

Principle: normative property of ALL systems in a context (general, e.g., 'services are stateless'). Requirement: property of ONE specific system. Requirements realize principles for a concrete system.

Driver: condition that motivates change (internal or external, e.g., 'customer satisfaction', 'NIS2 compliance' — a Network and Information Security directive). Goal: the intended end state the organization sets in response ('achieve NIS2 compliance by Q4').

notes.front: Business Object vs. Data Object vs. Artifact vs. Representation — distinguish
notes.back: Business object: conceptual domain notion ('Policy'). Data object: logically structured data ('Policy record') — realizes the business object. Artifact: physical piece of data ('policy.parquet') — realizes the data object. Representation: perceptible form for humans ('printed policy document') — realizes the business object.

notes.front: Node vs. Device vs. System Software vs. Equipment — distinguish
notes.back: Node: generic computational/physical resource. Device: physical IT hardware (specialization of node). System software: software execution environment (specialization of node). Equipment: physical machines working on MATERIALS (physical extension, also a node specialization).

notes.front: Path vs. Communication Network vs. Distribution Network — distinguish
notes.back: Path: logical link over which nodes exchange data/energy/material. Communication network: physical data-communication infrastructure that REALIZES paths. Distribution network: physical network transporting materials or energy (physical layer).

Collaboration: (active structure) two or more active elements aggregated to work together. Interaction: (behavior) the collective behavior the collaboration performs. Collaboration is assigned to the interaction.
Service: WHAT is offered — explicitly defined exposed behavior. Interface: WHERE/HOW it is accessed — the point of access (channel). The interface is assigned to the service it exposes.
Business service: a single unit of externally visible behavior. Product: a composite that aggregates one or more services, passive structure elements, and a contract, offered as a whole to customers.
Plateau: a stable STATE of the architecture during a period. Deliverable: a precisely-defined RESULT of a work package; deliverables realize plateaus.
